claim: SPRR1B and SPRR2A were induced in human sebocytes by exposure to lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: SPRR1B and SPPR2A were induced in human sebocytes by exposure to the bacterial cell wall component lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1A), qRT-PCR results (Figure 1B), and Western blot analysis (Figure 1C, D) showing increased SPRR expression after LPS treatment in SZ95 sebocyte cells.

claim: Colonization of germ-free mice was insufficient to trigger increased SPRR expression in mouse skin.
source: Colonization of germ-free mice was insufficient to trigger increased SPRR expression in mouse skin
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing similar Sprr gene expression between germ-free and conventional mice (Figure 2A).

claim: LPS injected into mouse skin stimulated increased expression of Sprr1a and Sprr2a through activation of MYD88.
source: but LPS injected into mouse skin stimulated increased expression of the mouse SPRR orthologous genes, Sprr1a and Sprr2a, through activation of MYD88.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing LPS-induced Sprr expression in wild-type but not Myd88−/− mice (Figure 2B).

claim: Both mouse and human SPRR proteins displayed potent bactericidal activity against MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and skin commensals.
source: Both mouse and human SPRR proteins displayed potent bactericidal activity against MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and skin commensals.
evidence: Supported by in vitro bacterial killing assays showing dose-dependent reduction in bacterial viability (Figure 3A, B).

claim: Sprr1a−/−;Sprr2a−/− mice are more susceptible to MRSA and P. aeruginosa skin infection.
source: Thus, Sprr1a−/−;Sprr2a−/− mice are more susceptible to MRSA and P. aeruginosa skin infection.
evidence: Supported by in vivo bioluminescent imaging showing greater bacterial burdens in knockout mice compared to wild-type (Figure 4A-F).

claim: SPRR proteins exert their bactericidal activity through binding and disruption of the bacterial membrane.
source: Lastly, mechanistic studies demonstrate that SPRR proteins exert their bactericidal activity through binding and disruption of the bacterial membrane.
evidence: Supported by propidium iodide uptake assays (Figure 3D), lipid binding assays (Figure 3E), and liposome disruption assays (Figure 3F).

claim: LPS treatment of SZ95 cells resulted in significant increase in SPRR1B, SPRR2A, and SPRR2D transcript abundance.
source: Consistent with our RNA-seq results, LPS-treated SZ95 cells displayed significant increase in the relative expression of SPRR family genes compared to vehicle-treated cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 1 μg LPS is optimal for induction of SPRR family genes expression.
source: Additionally, dose–response and time course experiments revealed that 1 μg LPS is optimal for induction of SPRR family genes expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two ligands of TLR2 (Pam3CSK4 and FSL-1) stimulate the expression of SPRR1B, SPRR2A, and SPRR2D genes in human sebocytes.
source: Interestingly, two ligands of TLR2 (Pam3CSK4 and FSL-1) stimulate the expression of SPRR1B, SPRR2A, and SPRR2D genes in human sebocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: LPS is a pattern-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) known to trigger gene transcription through the pattern recognition receptor, TLR4.
source: LPS is a pattern-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) known to trigger gene transcription through the pattern recognition receptor, TLR4 (Vaishnava et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vaishnava et al., 2011.

claim: Only Gram-negative bacteria tested could trigger SPRR2A expression in SZ95 sebocytes.
source: Interestingly, only the Gram-negative bacteria tested could trigger SPRR2A expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both live and heat-inactivated Escherichia coli bacteria were able to induce SPRR expression in mouse skin.
source: Consistent with these data, both live and heat-inactivated Escherichia coli bacteria were able to induce SPRR expression, suggesting that stimulation of Sprr1a and Sprr2a in mouse skin does not depend on the presence of bacterial metabolites (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stimulation of Sprr1a and Sprr2a in mouse skin does not depend on the presence of bacterial metabolites.
source: Consistent with these data, both live and heat-inactivated Escherichia coli bacteria were able to induce SPRR expression, suggesting that stimulation of Sprr1a and Sprr2a in mouse skin does not depend on the presence of bacterial metabolites (Figure 2C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both live and heat-inactivated E. coli induce SPRR expression equally.

claim: Sprr1a and Sprr2a transcript abundance is locally induced by crosshatch skin wounding in mice.
source: As has been shown by others (Vermeij and Backendorf, 2010), we also found that Sprr1a and Sprr2a transcript abundance is locally induced by crosshatch skin wounding in mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Vermeij and Backendorf, 2010.

claim: SPRR1A is expressed in the sebaceous gland and nonspecifically at the junction of the sebaceous gland and hair follicle.
source: SPRR1A is expressed in the SG and nonspecifically at the junction of the SG and hair follicle (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SPRR proteins expressed in the sebocyte may be secreted to the hair canal and are present at the skin surface.
source: This suggests SPRR proteins expressed in the sebocyte may be secreted to the hair canal and are present at the skin surface.
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence localization pattern shown in Figure 2E.

claim: LPS cannot induce the expression of SPRR family genes in human keratinocytes.
source: The qRT-PCR results showed that LPS cannot induce the expression of SPRR family genes in human keratinocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hTert cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LPS did not stimulate the increased expression of Sprr genes in mouse keratinocytes under either low or high calcium conditions.
source: However, LPS did not stimulate the increased expression of Sprr genes in mouse keratinocytes under either condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data from primary mouse keratinocytes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In primary keratinocytes high calcium conditions triggered increased expression of both mouse Sprr1a and Sprr2a.
source: Thus, in primary keratinocytes high calcium conditions triggered increased expression of both mouse Sprr1a and Sprr2a (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: SPRR proteins had no impact on the viability of E. coli.
source: In contrast, SPRR proteins had no impact on the viability of the prototypical Gram-negative bacteria E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by bacterial killing assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SPRR proteins cause distinct bacterial cell membrane damage and cytoplasmic leakage in P. aeruginosa.
source: Lastly, to visualize morphological changes of P. aeruginosa after exposure to SPRR proteins, we used transmission electron microscopy and observed distinct bacterial cell membrane damage and cytoplasmic leakage (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Human SPRR1B and mouse SPRR1A proteins promoted the dose-dependent uptake of propidium iodide by P. aeruginosa.
source: Human SPRR1B and mouse SPRR1A proteins promoted the dose-dependent uptake of the membrane-impermeant small molecule dye, PI, by P. aeruginosa (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by PI uptake assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both human SPRR1B and mouse SPRR1A bind to lipids bearing negatively charged lipid head groups, but not to neutral lipids.
source: Both human SPRR1B and mouse SPRR1A bind to lipids bearing negatively charged lipid head groups, but not to neutral lipids (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by lipid strip assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Most bacterial cell membranes are negatively charged and thus potentially susceptible to SPRR1 binding.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that most bacterial cell membranes are negatively charged and thus potentially susceptible to SPRR1 binding.
evidence: Inferred from lipid binding data and established knowledge about bacterial membrane composition.

claim: Both human SPRR1B and mouse SPRR1A protein-induced rapid dye efflux from negatively charged PC/PS liposomes in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Both human SPRR1B and mouse SPRR1A protein-induced rapid dye efflux from negatively charged PC/PS liposomes in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by liposome disruption assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Sprr1a−/−;Sprr2a−/− mice were healthy and showed normal skin barrier with no signs of immune infiltration and no significant change in transepidermal water loss (TEWL).
source: Sprr1a−/−;Sprr2a−/− mice were healthy and showed normal skin barrier with no signs of immune infiltration and no significant change in transepidermal water loss (TEWL) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by TEWL measurements and H&E staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice devoid of SPRR1A and SPRR2A expression had greater bacterial burdens in the first 3 days of MRSA infection.
source: Mice devoid of SPRR1A and SPRR2A expression had greater bacterial burdens in the first 3 days of MRSA infection (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescent imaging data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Sprr1a−/−;Sprr2a−/− mice are more susceptible to P. aeruginosa skin infection.
source: Intravital imaging and quantification revealed that Sprr1a−/−;Sprr2a−/− mice are more susceptible to P. aeruginosa skin infection (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescent imaging data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Skin is in direct contact with the microbe-filled outer world.
source: Skin is in direct contact with the microbe-filled outer world.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about skin anatomy and function.

claim: Defending the host from invasion by pathogens like S. aureus and P. aeruginosa is one of the chief functions of the skin.
source: Thus, defending the host from invasion by pathogens like S. aureus and P. aeruginosa is one of the chief functions of the skin (Kahn and Goldstein, 2016; Grice et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kahn and Goldstein, 2016 and Grice et al., 2008.

claim: SPRR proteins are upregulated in the GI tract, urinary tract, and the airway after exposure to stress and other inflammatory stimuli.
source: Several earlier studies have shown that SPRR proteins are upregulated in the GI tract, urinary tract, and the airway after exposure to stress and other inflammatory stimuli (Demetris et al., 2008; Hooper et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Demetris et al., 2008 and Hooper et al., 2001.

claim: SPRR2A has antimicrobial actions in the gastrointestinal tract during helminth infection.
source: Further, Hu et al. recently revealed that SPRR2A has antimicrobial actions in the gastrointestinal tract during helminth infection (Hu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2021.

claim: Sebum secretion can act as a delivery system for AMPs.
source: Sebum secretion can also act as a delivery system for AMPs (Lovászi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lovászi et al., 2017.

claim: AMPs can damage mammalian membranes.
source: Though beneficial to the host, AMPs can damage mammalian membranes, so confining expression of AMPs to the nonviable parts of skin through sebum delivery is optimal.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about AMP properties.

claim: Sebum excretes AMPs to the surface within an acidic milieu, which is often required for AMP activity.
source: Sebum also excretes AMPs to the surface within an acidic milieu, which is often required for AMP activity (Malik et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Malik et al., 2016.

claim: Colonization of germ-free mice is sufficient to stimulate SPRR2A expression in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: These finding are distinct from what has been observed in the gastrointestinal tract, where colonization of germ-free mice is sufficient to stimulate SPRR2A expression (Hu et al., 2021; Hooper et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2021 and Hooper et al., 2001.

claim: SPRR family proteins function as crosslinking proteins in terminal differentiation of keratinocytes and formation of the cornified cell envelope.
source: As SPRR family proteins also function as crosslinking proteins in terminal differentiation of keratinocytes and formation of the cornified cell envelope (Candi et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Candi et al., 2005.

claim: Skin devoid of SPRR1 and SPRR2 was more susceptible to skin infection by MRSA and P. aeruginosa, both pathogens that cause skin infections requiring hospitalization.
source: Though SPRR1 was ineffective against E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), skin devoid of SPRR1 and SPRR2 was more susceptible to skin infection by MRSA and P. aeruginosa, both pathogens that cause skin infections requiring hospitalization (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 4 and established knowledge about MRSA and P. aeruginosa as pathogens.

claim: The antimicrobial function of proline-rich proteins has been described in other organisms.
source: Our findings that SPRR family proteins have antimicrobial function may have implications for other proline-rich proteins expressed in human skin, as the antimicrobial function of proline-rich proteins has been described in other organisms (Scocchi et al., 2011; Stotz et al., 2009; Welch et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scocchi et al., 2011; Stotz et al., 2009; Welch et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014.

claim: Human skin functions as a physical barrier, preventing the entry of foreign pathogens while also accommodating a myriad of commensal microorganisms.
source: Human skin functions as a physical barrier, preventing the entry of foreign pathogens while also accommodating a myriad of commensal microorganisms.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about skin function.

claim: Mice devoid of sebocytes are prone to skin infection.
source: Mice devoid of sebocytes are prone to skin infection, yet our understanding of how sebocytes function in host defense is incomplete.
evidence: Based on prior research cited in the context of the study.

claim: The skin surface continuously encounters a diverse microbial community including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites.
source: As a result, the skin surface continuously encounters a diverse microbial community including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites (Duerkop and Hooper, 2013; Oh et al., 2016; Findley et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duerkop and Hooper, 2013; Oh et al., 2016; Findley et al., 2013.

claim: Skin and soft tissue infections pose a considerable public health threat.
source: Thus, skin and soft tissue infections pose a considerable public health threat (Dryden, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dryden, 2009.

claim: The majority of infections of the skin are caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
source: The majority of infections of the skin are caused by Staphylococcus aureus (Kahn and Goldstein, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kahn and Goldstein, 2016.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in burn patients are one of the most common causes of mortality.
source: Additionally, Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in burn patients are one of the most common causes of mortality (Huebinger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huebinger et al., 2016.

claim: Skin antimicrobial proteins (AMPs) play an essential role in defending the host from the invasion of pathogens.
source: Skin antimicrobial proteins (AMPs) play an essential role in defending the host from the invasion of pathogens (Zhang and Gallo, 2016; Nakatsuji and Gallo, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang and Gallo, 2016; Nakatsuji and Gallo, 2012.

claim: Mammalian AMPs are evolutionarily ancient immune effectors that rapidly kill bacteria by targeting bacterial cell wall or cell membrane structures.
source: Mammalian AMPs are evolutionarily ancient immune effectors that rapidly kill bacteria by targeting bacterial cell wall or cell membrane structures (Mukherjee et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mukherjee et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2018.

claim: Several distinct AMP families, such as β-defensins, cathelicidins, resistin, and S100 proteins, have been identified and characterized in skin.
source: Several distinct AMP families, such as β-defensins, cathelicidins, resistin, and S100 proteins, have been identified and characterized in skin (Gallo and Hooper, 2012; Harris et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gallo and Hooper, 2012; Harris et al., 2019.

claim: Sebaceous glands (SGs) are specialized epithelial cells that cover the entire skin surface except the palms and soles.
source: Sebaceous glands (SGs) are specialized epithelial cells that cover the entire skin surface except the palms and soles.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about sebaceous glands.

claim: SGs excrete a lipid-rich and waxy substance called sebum to the skin surface.
source: SGs excrete a lipid-rich and waxy substance called sebum to the skin surface (Fischer et al., 2017; Zouboulis et al., 2020; Zouboulis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2017; Zouboulis et al., 2020; Zouboulis et al., 2016.

claim: SGs are believed to contribute to the antimicrobial functions of the skin.
source: SGs are believed to contribute to the antimicrobial functions of the skin (Gallo and Hooper, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallo and Hooper, 2012.

claim: Human SPRR proteins are 6–18 kDa in size and comprise four subclasses (SPRR1, SPRR2, SPRR3, and SPRR4) with a similar structural organization.
source: Human SPRR proteins are 6–18 kDa in size and comprise four subclasses (SPRR1, SPRR2, SPRR3, and SPRR4) with a similar structural organization.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SPRR protein structure.

claim: Two SPRR1 and seven SPRR2 proteins are characterized with a much higher homogeneity, as they contain a similar consensus repeat sequence.
source: Among them, two SPRR1 and seven SPRR2 proteins are characterized with a much higher homogeneity, as they contain a similar consensus repeat sequence (Cabral et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cabral et al., 2001.

claim: SPRR proteins were originally identified in skin as markers of terminal differentiation that function as substrates of transglutaminase in the crosslinked cornified envelope present at the skin surface.
source: SPRR proteins were originally identified in skin as markers of terminal differentiation that function as substrates of transglutaminase in the crosslinked cornified envelope present at the skin surface (Cabral et al., 2001; Candi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cabral et al., 2001; Candi et al., 2005.

claim: LPS had broad impacts on gene expression in human sebocytes, including the increased expression of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and AMPs.
source: LPS, which coats the surface of Gram-negative bacteria, had broad impacts on gene expression in human sebocytes, including the increased expression of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and AMPs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Three members of the small proline-rich family of proteins (SPRR) were markedly upregulated in sebocytes after LPS treatment.
source: Notably, three members of the small proline-rich family of proteins (SPRR) were markedly upregulated in sebocytes after LPS treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SPRR proteins expression increased after LPS treatment in SZ95 cells.
source: Consistent with the qRT-PCR results, SPRR proteins expression also increased after LPS treatment in SZ95 cells (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: Sebocytes respond to bacterial lipoproteins by expressing SPRR1 and SPRR2 proteins.
source: Interestingly, two ligands of TLR2 (Pam3CSK4 and FSL-1) stimulate the expression of SPRR1B, SPRR2A, and SPRR2D genes in human sebocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that sebocytes respond to these bacterial lipoproteins by expressing SPRR1 and SPRR2 proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TLR2 ligands stimulate SPRR expression.

claim: Bacterial colonization alone is insufficient to trigger increased expression of Sprr genes in mouse skin.
source: In contrast to what we observed in human sebocytes in culture, Sprr gene expression was similar between germ-free and conventional mice (Figure 2A), indicating that bacterial colonization alone is insufficient to trigger increased expression of Sprr genes in mouse skin.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LPS induces SPRR protein expression through the TLR-MYD88 signaling pathway.
source: Thus, LPS injected into the skin of Myd88−/− mice did not trigger increased expression of the SPRR genes (Figure 2B), indicating that LPS induces SPRR protein expression through the TLR-MYD88 signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data comparing wild-type and Myd88−/− mice shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SPRR1A and SPRR2A are expressed by keratinocytes.
source: Since our immunofluorescence images and prior studies in keratinocytes indicated that SPRR1A and SPRR2A are expressed by keratinocytes (Fischer et al., 1996; Sark et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and citations to Fischer et al., 1996; Sark et al., 1998.

claim: In primary keratinocytes, high calcium conditions are required for differentiation in culture.
source: Under low calcium conditions, keratinocytes proliferate but require higher calcium conditions to differentiate in culture.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about keratinocyte culture conditions.

claim: Bacterial colonization and LPS treatment of keratinocytes in culture were not sufficient to augment SPRR expression in the skin.
source: Taken together, these data show that SPRR proteins are upregulated by LPS in human sebocytes in culture and by LPS injection in mouse skin. Bacterial colonization and LPS treatment of keratinocytes in culture were not sufficient to augment SPRR expression in the skin.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental results from Figures 2A and 2—figure supplements 1-2.

claim: The SPRR family of proteins have highly conserved amino acid sequences with numerous cysteine and proline repeats.
source: The SPRR family of proteins have highly conserved amino acid sequences with numerous cysteine and proline repeats.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SPRR protein structure.

claim: In insects and lower vertebrates, proteins rich in cysteines and prolines have been shown to kill microbes.
source: However, in insects and lower vertebrates, proteins rich in cysteines and prolines have been shown to kill microbes (Scocchi et al., 2011; Stotz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scocchi et al., 2011; Stotz et al., 2009.

claim: When bacteria were exposed to SPRR proteins, there was a marked dose-dependent reduction in the viability of Staphylococcus epidermidis, MRSA, and P. aeruginosa.
source: When bacteria were exposed to SPRR proteins, we observed a marked dose-dependent reduction in the viability of Staphylococcus epidermidis, MRSA, and P. aeruginosa (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by bacterial killing assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a more than 90% decline in bacterial viability after 2-hr exposure to 2.5 µM of SPRR proteins.
source: with a more than 90% decline in bacterial viability after 2-hr exposure to 2.5 µM of SPRR proteins (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by bacterial killing assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Penetration of bacterial stimuli to deeper portions of the skin may be required for MYD88-mediated SPRR protein production in skin.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that penetration of bacterial stimuli to deeper portions of the skin may be required for MYD88-mediated SPRR protein production in skin.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that intradermal LPS injection, but not colonization, induces SPRR expression.

claim: Confining expression of AMPs to the nonviable parts of skin through sebum delivery is optimal.
source: Though beneficial to the host, AMPs can damage mammalian membranes, so confining expression of AMPs to the nonviable parts of skin through sebum delivery is optimal.
evidence: Logical inference based on the properties of AMPs and sebum delivery.

claim: There are likely other regulatory networks that control SPRR protein expression in skin in response to wounding and other stimuli.
source: As SPRR family proteins also function as crosslinking proteins in terminal differentiation of keratinocytes and formation of the cornified cell envelope (Candi et al., 2005), there are likely other regulatory networks that control SPRR protein expression in skin in response to wounding and other stimuli.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the multiple functions of SPRR proteins.

claim: SPRR proteins might be promising alternatives to traditional antibiotics used to cure MRSA or P. aeruginosa infection.
source: SPRR proteins might be promising alternatives to traditional antibiotics used to cure MRSA or P. aeruginosa infection.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the antimicrobial activity demonstrated in the study.

claim: SPRR1 and SPRR2 proteins function as AMPs in the skin.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that SPRR1 and SPRR2 proteins function as AMPs in the skin.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including bacterial killing assays and infection studies.

claim: SPRR proteins protect against pathogenic bacterial infections of the skin.
source: Sprr1a−/−;Sprr2a−/− mice are more susceptible to MRSA and P. aeruginosa skin infection, revealing that SPRR proteins protect against pathogenic bacterial infections of the skin.
evidence: Supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The bactericidal activity of SPRR proteins is mediated through the binding and disruption of bacterial membranes.
source: We also show mechanistically that the bactericidal activity of SPRR proteins is mediated through the binding and disruption of bacterial membranes.
evidence: Supported by PI uptake, lipid binding, and liposome disruption assays shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: SPRR proteins have potent bactericidal activity against Staphylococcal species and the Gram-negative bacteria P. aeruginosa with effective inhibition at low micromolar concentrations.
source: In this study, we also reveal that SPRR family proteins have potent bactericidal activity against Staphylococcal species and the Gram-negative bacteria P. aeruginosa (Figure 3A–C), with effective inhibition at low micromolar concentrations.
evidence: Supported by bacterial killing assay data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Mouse and human SPRR1 proteins interact with negatively charged lipid membranes, suggesting broader spectrum antimicrobial capability of these proteins.
source: Further, our biochemical data show that mouse and human SPRR1 proteins interact with negatively charged lipid membranes, suggesting broader spectrum antimicrobial capability of these proteins (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Supported by lipid binding and liposome disruption data shown in Figure 3D-F, with inference about broader antimicrobial capability.

claim: Damaged or burned skin has increased risk of P. aeruginosa infection.
source: Since damaged or burned skin has increased risk of P. aeruginosa infection (Huebinger et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Huebinger et al., 2016.

claim: Treatments for MRSA and P. aeruginosa infections are currently limited.
source: Treatments for these infections are currently limited.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about antibiotic resistance and treatment challenges.
